stage_2_story.text_en: On a rainy Thursday, Avi took his two children to the city's art museum for the first time. They had passed it a hundred times but never gone inside. The moment they walked through the door, his daughter Maya pointed at a bronze sculpture in the lobby — a tall, twisted figure reaching toward the ceiling — and asked if they could touch it. The security guard smiled and shook his head. A young curator met them at the entrance and offered to lead a short tour. She guided them through the permanent collection on the ground floor, explaining which pieces were donations and which had been purchased over the decades. In the second room, they stopped before a large abstract canvas. His son Omer could not decide if he liked it or not. 'It looks like someone spilled paint,' he said. The curator laughed and explained that the artist had done exactly that — on purpose. Upstairs, a temporary exhibit featured work by a local painter who had lived nearby a century ago. One portrait in the corner stopped Avi completely. The woman in the painting stared back at him with such stillness that he stood there for five minutes without speaking. The curator told them that the portrait was considered the painter's masterpiece, and that it had been bought by a generous patron fifty years ago and donated to the museum shortly after. By the time they reached the gift shop, even Omer had changed his mind about modern art. On the bus home, Maya said she wanted to buy a canvas and paint something abstract herself. Avi thought that was the best idea he had heard all week.
